newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-S.Africa's Stals has no weak rand policy.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-S.Africa's Stals has no weak rand policy.

text.p: South Africa's Reserve Bank governor Chris Stals said on Thursday the bank had no pre-determined policy of allowing the rand to weaken.
In an interview, Stals said recent rand weakness followed negative sentiment towards emerging markets in general, and declines in the price of gold.
Asked if the central bank had a predetermined policy of allowing the rand to depreciate, Stals said:

"No, certainly that is not our policy. We still lean against the wind, we intervene in the markets. We've been buying foreign exchange for some time now to prevent the rand from appreciating more, but with the main purpose to provide liquidity to the market, to smooth out fluctuations and to add to the foreign reserves of the Reserve Bank."
But he also said that the rand was not a candidate for appreciation.

"Since the end of October last year the rand appreciated for a five-six month period up to the end of March. So in the longer term the rand is not really a candidate for appreciating, taking into account our rate of inflation and cost of production and competitiveness in the world."

Foreign exchange traders on Wednesday speculated that the Reserve Bank had been buying dollars to engineer a weaker rand because of concerns about the effects the weaker gold price would have on its reserves and the country's export proceeds, but this was denied by deputy governor James Cross.
The rand weakened three cents to 4.56 to the dollar in the three days to the close on Wednesday, but picked up to 4.5500/5530 by noon on Thursday.
Stals also said in the interview with Reuters Financial Television he was reluctant to cut interest rates without a slowdown in money supply and credit growth.
"The Reserve Bank will not take the lead to bring interest rates down unless there will be some slowdown in the rate of increase in the money supply and in bank credit extension," he said.
He said both had levelled out in the last few months but there was no confirmation yet that they were moving down to lower levels.
South Africa's key bank rate is 17 percent, having been raised from 16 percent in November 1996.
Preliminary May M3 money supply growth was 15.40 percent, little changed from a month before, while private sector credit growth slowed to 16.57 percent from 17.4 percent in the same period.
A Reuter poll of economists late in June said a one percentage point cut in rates was possible by the end of the third quarter and was a certainty by the end of the year.
Stals said the July 1 relaxation of foreign exchange controls on individuals had resulted in minimal outflows so far despite initial fears that it could lead to substantial short term capital flight.

"The experience for the first two weeks was that it is very small. For the first 10 days or so the amount was only 25 million rand," Stals said. "So South Africans are fortunately not rushing in to take money out of the country at this stage."
